https://telex.hu/after/2026/08/13/megala.text: Menü Kereső Új bizottság dönt a magyar Oscar-nevezésről After Patakfalvi Dóra A Nemzeti Filmintézet a Filmreform 2026-tal együttműködve kért fel elismert filmes szakembereket abba a testületbe, amely a magyar Oscar-nevezésről dönt a következő időszakban. A bizottság új tagjai: Erdély Mátyás operatőr; Gazdag Gyula forgatókönyvíró-rendező; Gelencsér Gábor filmtörténész, kritikus; Kocsis Ágnes rendező; László Sára producer; Horváth Kristóf fesztiváligazgató, a fiatal filmesek képviseletében. Az Amerikai Filmakadémia jövő március 14-én 99. alkalommal rendezi meg az Oscar-díjátadó gálát, a nemzetközi film kategóriában pedig minden ország nevezhet egy egész estés filmet azok közül, amelyeket 2025. október 1. és 2026. szeptember 30. között hét egymást követő napon át játszottak az adott országban kereskedelmi moziforgalmazásban. Az országok hivatalos nevezései közül az Amerikai Filmakadémia képviselői választják ki a jelölt filmeket január elején. A legjobb nemzetközi filmnek járó Oscar-díjról végül az Amerikai Filmakadémia teljes tagsága szavaz. 2025-ben a Nemzeti Filmintézet döntése alapján Nemes Jeles László Árva című alkotását nevezte Magyarország Oscarra a legjobb nemzetközi film kategóriájában. Az akkori bizottság tagjai Csáky Attila producer, Káel Csaba mozgóképipari kormánybiztos, Koltai Lajos operatőr-rendező, Lukácsy György dramaturg-rendező, Novák Emil operatőr-rendező, a Magyar Filmakadémia elnöke, Pesti Ákos filmgyártási szakember és Szabó Csilla dramaturg volt. Az Árva végül nem került be az Amerikai Filmakadémia rövid listájába. Kövess minket Facebookon is! Követem! Friss az Afteren

https://www.politico.eu/article/france-p.text: PARIS — The Paris prosecutor’s office has launched an investigation into disinformation efforts targeting two prominent candidates in France’s upcoming presidential election, according to Agence France-Presse . Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, two former prime ministers who are high-profile contenders for the 2027 race, were reportedly the subject earlier this summer of fake news reports posted on social media aimed at undermining their campaigns. Fabricated videos posted on X that used branding from leading French news platforms claimed Philippe, who suffers from alopecia, was diagnosed with a neurodegenerative disease, while fake reports on X and TikTok alleged Attal had Parkinson’s disease and was using drugs. Advertisement Advertisement Attal denounced the reports as fake and filed a complaint. Philippe has refrained from publicly commenting on the posts, though his top allies have framed them as likely Russian interference. France’s specialized agency in charge of monitoring online foreign interference, Viginum, has pointed to Russia-affiliated networks Storm-1516 and Matriochka as likely suspects for the disinformation operations targeting Philippe and Attal, respectively. Center-left MEP and likely presidential contender Raphaël Glucksmann was also targeted by a similar disinformation operation . The prosecutor’s office announced the launch of a separate probe into that case earlier this month.

https://newswire.net/business/last-minut.text: Business Last-Minute Cleaning in Bratislava: When the Visit Has To Happen Today By Barbara Brown 2026-08-31 Some cleaning requirements arrive with notice and some arrive with none. A viewing scheduled for tomorrow morning, a guest confirming a booking four hours before check-in, an inspection brought forward, family arriving a day early. In those situations the question is not which cleaning tier is optimal — it is whether anyone can come at all. Last-minute cleaning in Bratislava from Shine Guards is priced and organised specifically for that constraint. What the Urgent Option Is Shine Guards lists urgent cleaning with dispatch within two hours at €30 per hour. It is described as Last-Minute Cleaning — the service for situations that cannot wait for a scheduled slot. The two-hour dispatch window is the defining parameter. It is not a promise to complete the work within two hours; it is a commitment to have a specialist on the way within that time, which is the part that actually determines whether the situation is recoverable. Hourly pricing is used here rather than the fixed-quote model applied to the standard tiers, because an urgent booking is accepted before the property can be assessed. The rate is published, so the client can still calculate the cost from an estimate of the hours. The scope is agreed on the call. With limited time, the sensible approach is to prioritise rather than to specify a full clean — kitchen and bathroom first, visible surfaces and floors next, everything else if time allows. Availability follows the contact centre hours: Monday to Friday from 09:00 to 18:00 and at weekends from 10:00 to 16:00. Requests submitted in that window are handled immediately; outside it, the following opening. The Situations It Exists For Property viewings arranged at short notice. Estate agents work on the availability of buyers and tenants, not owners, and a viewing confirmed for the next morning leaves no room for a scheduled clean. Short-term rental turnovers that slip. A late check-out, a cleaner who cannot make it, or a same-day booking confirmed after the previous guest has left all produce the same problem: a check-in in a few hours and an apartment that is not ready. Inspections brought forward. Landlord visits, agency checks and handover appointments move, and the notice period is often measured in hours. Unexpected guests. Family arriving a day early or a stay extended into a spare room that has been storing everything else for six months. Post-event cleaning. A gathering that ended later and messier than planned, with a working day starting in the morning. Illness or injury in a household that normally handles its own cleaning, where the routine simply stops and someone else has to pick it up quickly. How to Get the Most Out of a Short Visit Prioritise before the specialist arrives. Decide which two rooms actually matter. In almost every scenario the answer is the kitchen and the bathroom, because those are the rooms a visitor, guest or inspector evaluates. Clear surfaces in advance if there is time. Cleaning time spent moving objects is time not spent cleaning, and a client who clears the countertops buys back a meaningful share of the visit. Be specific on the call. “Kitchen, main bathroom, hallway floor, and the living room if there is time” is a workable brief. “Everything, quickly” is not, and it produces a thin result everywhere instead of a good result somewhere. Say what the visit is for. A clean before a viewing prioritises visible impression — floors, glass, surfaces, smells. A clean before a handover prioritises the items a landlord inspects: limescale, grease, appliance interiors. The order of work should differ. Do not add extras to an urgent booking unless they are the reason for it. An oven at €35 makes sense before a handover inspection; it does not make sense when the goal is a presentable flat in ninety minutes. Settle access immediately. Key, code, building entry, parking — an urgent visit loses its advantage entirely if the specialist arrives and cannot get in. How Urgent Differs From the Standard Tiers Standard bookings run on fixed pricing agreed in advance, with the figure set before dispatch and unchanged afterwards. The urgent option runs on a published hourly rate because there is no time to assess the property first. Standard bookings are scheduled around the client — mornings, evenings or weekends — with the date agreed during the confirmation call. Urgent bookings are scheduled around availability, which is the trade-off being paid for. Standard bookings follow a defined scope by tier: Basic for maintenance, Full-Scale for a refresh, Deep for an intensive reset. Urgent bookings follow a priority list agreed verbally. What does not change is the standard of work. The same trained specialists carry out both, each having completed training and passed a practical assessment before working independently with clients. Responsibility also does not change. The company takes responsibility for the property during the visit, and if something is damaged, it accepts responsibility and resolves the issue. Nor does the follow-up. The manager checks the result afterwards, and anything not done correctly is corrected without an additional charge. Reducing the Need for Urgent Bookings A recurring schedule is the structural answer. A property on a weekly or fortnightly maintenance cycle is never more than a few days from presentable, which converts most emergencies into minor inconveniences. Short-term rental hosts benefit most from this, since their exposure is highest. A standing turnover arrangement with the same specialist assigned where possible removes the majority of same-day failures. Landlords with multiple units gain the same effect by keeping a provider on file rather than sourcing one when a tenancy ends unexpectedly. Property owners preparing to sell should book the intensive clean early rather than before the first viewing. Viewings then require touch-ups instead of interventions. Where urgent bookings remain necessary, having the account already set up — property parameters known, access arrangements agreed, payment method established — turns a complicated call into a short one. Booking and Contacts Urgent cleaning, the three standard tiers, extra services and the online cost calculator are all published at https://www.shineguards.com/bratislava/ , with the scope and rates listed per service. For an urgent request, direct contact is faster than the form: +43 1 442 10 36 or hello@shineguards.com, with WhatsApp and Telegram on +43 681 20873649. The contact centre works Monday to Friday 09:00–18:00 and at weekends 10:00–16:00. Standard requests submitted through the form receive a manager call-back within roughly 30 minutes to confirm parameters and fix the price and date. New clients receive a 10% welcome bonus on a first order, and new commercial clients — including short-term rental operators and property managers — receive their first cleaning free of charge. Payment is taken after the service in cash, by card or by cashless transfer. Shine Guards e.U. is registered at Stoß im Himmel 1/21, 1010 Vienna, and works in Bratislava alongside Vienna, Graz and Munich. https://www.politico.eu/article/kaja-kal.text: While actively running the EU’s foreign policy on the world’s most demanding issues, Kaja Kallas still finds time outside work to read about … more foreign policy. The top EU diplomat and former Estonian prime minister frequently talks about her love of reading, citing her favorite authors in speeches and meeting with them privately to discuss their work. Since taking up her most recent post in December 2024, she has read at least 52 books she has shared publicly — all of which she has posted on her Instagram — most of them related to international affairs. In total, she has shared more than 200 titles since 2017. “You know, my reading list is quite long,” said Kallas, who officially serves as the high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy, at a press conference in January. “By the end, when I finish this job, I will be very smart,” she joked. Advertisement The collection closely tracks the subjects Kallas is most involved with in her role, evolving alongside her professional remit: 24 books on Russia and Ukraine, nine on China, and seven on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Further-flung regions pop up only rarely, with just three books on the rest of East Asia and none on South American politics beyond Venezuela. “Reading books is a valuable advantage, especially as it is not so common nowadays,” an official from Kallas’ team told POLITICO. “The Middle East wars, Russia’s aggression and China’s growing influence are major geopolitical issues, so naturally they feature on the High Representative’s reading list.” Noting that she meets with ministers, officials, staff and experts daily and receives countless briefing papers, memos and other sources of information, “books are a nice addition on long-distance flights,” the official added. The reading lists alone have not shaped the full contours of Kallas’ foreign policy, of course. But they provide a view into which political subjects Europe’s chief diplomat is interested in learning more about and where she goes looking for answers. So, what does Kallas’ bookshelf reveal about the person shaping Europe’s diplomacy? To find out, POLITICO reviewed the 248 titles she has included on public reading lists since 2017 and spoke to 24 of the authors. Noted bookworm Kallas is not the only avid reader in Brussels, but few politicians talk about their love of literature quite as often. Since 2023, she has released reading lists twice a year on Instagram, and before that, she blogged about her latest reads monthly. “I read a lot, but you’re always influenced by the books you’ve read most recently,” Kallas told POLITICO in 2025. Political scientist Ivan Krastev, who co-authored 2019’s “The Light That Failed: A Reckoning” on why liberalism failed to spread in Eastern Europe, said Kallas had reached out to him after reading his book. She was trying to find a publisher to translate it into her native Estonian, he told POLITICO. The translation was eventually released in 2022. While Kallas was prime minister, her government had similarly pushed for the translation of political scientist Mark Leonard’s “The Age of Unpeace: How Connectivity Causes Conflict,” which she said she would “often cite.” “It’s interesting, particularly when a politician in a high position reads a book,” said Krastev. “They’re trying to make sense of their own experience” and “trying to answer some of the questions that [they] are struggling with.” Indeed, Kallas’ book choices appear to closely reflect her scheduled diplomatic trips. Visiting Montenegro for the EU-Western Balkans Summit in June this year, the top diplomat had read the memoirs of Richard Holbrooke, architect of the 1995 Dayton Accords in Bosnia, and Martti Ahtisaari, the former Finnish president and mediator of the 1999 Kumanovo Agreement forcing Serbia’s withdrawal from Kosovo. A post shared by Kaja Kallas (@kajakallas) “A lot to learn also today, and actually a lot of parallels,” said Kallas of Holbrooke’s book in July. Ahead of her trip to Sarajevo a month later, she then contacted former Swedish Prime Minister and High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina Carl Bildt about his 1998 book “Peace Journey: The Struggle for Peace in Bosnia,” a memoir about his work in the region. “She sent me a text and said, ‘I’m reading your book, and I like it very much.’ And I said, ‘How on earth did you get hold of that one?'” Bildt told POLITICO, joking that the book was published nearly three decades ago. “She wanted to go down into the weeds of the history … and that could be useful.” Earlier in the year, after the U.S. forcibly captured Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro, Kallas picked up two books about the South American country, too: “Comandante: Hugo Chávez’s Venezuela” and “Things Are Never So Bad That They Can’t Get Worse: Inside the Collapse of Venezuela.” “She is one of the best-read people I know,” said Marietje Schaake, a friend and former liberal MEP who served with Kallas in the European Parliament. “That depth has shaped her thinking and her career.” What’s in the library? Six of the authors who spoke to POLITICO for this article specifically cited Kallas’ hawkish stance on Moscow as echoing the messages in their books — perhaps unsurprising given Kallas warned of Russia’s threat to Europe back in 2021, during her first term as prime minister. “What is happening in Ukraine right now is what I was reading about in our own history books,” she told Vogue Greece in 2023. Sylvie Kauffmann, author of 2023’s “Blindsided” ( Les aveuglés ) — which argues that Germany and France failed to recognize the Russian threat — told POLITICO her book “confirms everything that Kallas thinks” about how others downplayed Moscow’s aggression. Speaking to POLITICO about his 2018 book “Identity,” famed political philosopher of liberal democracy Francis Fukuyama said the work contained “a kind of ideological roadmap to be able to better explain what it is that … we’re fighting for.” Noting that Ukraine’s fight against Russia was one of the reasons he wrote it, Fukuyama then praised the chief diplomat’s support for the country. Kallas has also read extensively on Israel-Palestine, a conflict on which her stance has attracted both attention and controversy in Brussels. Far more critical of Israel than her peers in the European Commission, Kallas reportedly compared the situation on the ground to South Africa under apartheid during a closed-door meeting in June, causing Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar to sever contact. Two of the authors on the subject who feature on Kallas’ reading lists told POLITICO her reported comparison mirrored the arguments made in their books, with 2024 Pulitzer Prize winner Nathan Thrall saying his “aim in writing [“A Day in the Life of Abed Salama: Anatomy of a Jerusalem Tragedy”] was to influence people like her.” “The fact that she has come to the conclusion that Israel is practicing apartheid is most welcome as far as I’m concerned,” he said. “I explain the aspects of apartheid, and I hope she’d see that her judgment is well founded,” echoed Michael Scott-Baumann, author of “Palestinians and Israelis: A Short History of Conflict.” But not every author on Kallas’ lists approves of her foreign policy decisions when it comes to their topics of specialization. Kim Ghattas, who wrote her book “Black Wave” on the Middle East, for example, said Kallas has been too passive on the Israeli-U.S. war with Iran. “That is not good policymaking. I would hope that reading books like mine can help prepare policymakers like her, specifically for moments like the one that we find ourselves in right now.” A post shared by Kaja Kallas (@kajakallas) Former U.S. National Security Adviser John Bolton, who has long advocated for regime change in Iran, said he, too, wished Kallas had become more involved — though in support of President Donald Trump’s military operation. He also noted that Kallas’ blunt style risked further alienating the U.S. from the EU, with her comments advocating for the bloc’s sovereignty “giving [Trump] the excuse to do what he probably wants to do anyway.” Criticism extended beyond the Middle East as well. Robert D. Kaplan, author of 1993’s “Balkan Ghosts” — which heavily influenced former U.S. President Bill Clinton’s initial reluctance to militarily intervene in the region, according to his biographers — told POLITICO that Kallas’ impolitic moments “may be things that she’ll come to partially regret over time.” “When you get far quick, you tend to make mistakes. Because you’re confident, you’re even arrogant,” said Kaplan. Booking ahead It’s not all about world affairs and global diplomacy, though — some of Kallas’ more recent political predicaments lie a little closer to home. Recent months have seen the top diplomat losing a turf war with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen over the bloc’s foreign policy, while her diplomatic service, the European External Action Service, has struggled to build consensus across a divided Europe. So with the rentrée almost upon us in Brussels, there may be no better time for Kallas to get through a few more books — a strategy she has turned to previously. While serving as prime minister, during a 2023 podcast, Kallas recalled how she once considered foreign policy to be her greatest political weakness — until she turned to books. “It’s not my weakness anymore because I’ve read so much about this,” she said. Perhaps this time it will be Brussels that sends her back to the stacks.

https://www.cei.int/ansa/180105.text: European security: in Karpacz deterrence and new threats in 2027 (ANSA) - KARPACZ, 11 SET - Central and Eastern Europe must prepare for a protracted standoff with Russia, which is set to take on different forms regardless of the outcome of the war in Ukraine. This is the scenario outlined for 2027 during the panel discussion 'A year of war? A year of peace? Security prospects for Central and Eastern Europe in 2027', organised as part of the 35th edition of the Karpacz Economic Forum in Poland. The debate, which focused on the prospects for peace and security in the region, was attended by representatives from institutions, the military, industry and the research sector in Poland, Lithuania, Portugal and Italy. At the heart of the discussion was the need to strengthen conventional deterrence and European defence industrial capacity, alongside resilience in the face of hybrid threats and greater strategic autonomy, whilst maintaining the transatlantic bond. "Europe must prepare for a protracted standoff and counterbalance Russian assertiveness," said Emanuele Errichiello, deputy director of the Centre for International Studies (CSI) and a Fellow at the London School of Economics. "Weakness invites the next show of force, whilst credible deterrence is what can persuade Moscow to reach an agreement that it will then be willing to honour," he added. According to Errichiello, European security must be considered "from all angles", including domains such as cyberspace, undersea cables, disinformation and the exploitation of migration flows. Particular attention was also paid to the southern flank and Russia's role in the Mediterranean. "The eastern and Mediterranean fronts are dimensions of a single, indivisible security space: the European one," emphasised Errichiello, identifying the resilience of European societies as "the most neglected aspect" of security. On the Polish side, contributions from representatives of the Armed Forces General Staff, Sławomir Walenczykowski; Polska Grupa Zbrojeniowa, Adam Leszkiewicz; and the Military University of Technology, represented by Robert Wozniak, emphasised the need to strengthen the industrial base and deterrence on the eastern flank. Jovitas Raskevicius, from the Special Investigation Service of the Republic of Lithuania, emphasised institutional resilience and hybrid threats, whilst the president of idD Portugal Defencem, Ricardo Pinheiro Alves, highlighted the need to strengthen European defence capabilities within the framework of the Atlantic Alliance. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw8d.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, State officials and others have criticised how Cornell and local prosecutors handled the case By Madeline Halpert Published 13 October 2026 Cornell University is banning all parties at fraternity houses as the school faces backlash over its handling of an alleged sexual assault on campus two years ago. Last month, a woman known as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit alleging she was plied with drugs and raped by several men in 2024 at a party at a Cornell fraternity house. In a statement on Tuesday, Cornell's president, Michael Kotlikoff, announced a series of measures responding to the alleged assault, including the end to fraternity parties for the rest of the school year. "I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community," he said. Figure caption, Cornell students voice frustration at public hearing over rape case "It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action," he added. Fraternities have existed at university campuses across the US for decades and function as all-male social clubs where the students live, study and socialise. Over the years, the groups have become notorious for binge-drinking, partying and dangerous hazing rituals. In a statement, a lawyer representing Doe said she filed a civil lawsuit "to achieve her aim of improving Cornell and its response to abuse claims". "While the steps announced today are helpful to achieve this goal, they are too late to protect Ms. Doe," said lawyer Thomas Giuffra. Cornell's president said anyone who violated the new fraternity party policy at the New York university would be suspended. The school also said it planned to improve support for survivors of sexual assault, including more staff to help people report sexual misconduct and navigate other support systems as well. Through Title IX, the federal law that governs how universities handle sexual assault claims, schools are required to provide measures of support to help survivors stay in school after assaults. Doe's lawyer has said she dropped out after the alleged assault. Cornell case highlights 'draining' maze for victims to report campus sex assaults The president said the school will allow New York State Police's trauma-informed officers to investigate allegations of sexual assault on its campus. These officers will interview survivors who want to pursue criminal charges and prepare "comprehensive investigative summaries for the appropriate law enforcement agency", Kotlikoff said. Cornell has faced criticism over the information shared with the local district attorney's office about Jane Doe's allegations. Out of hundreds of documents that US media outlets have obtained from Cornell's investigation into the assault, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said that in 2024, his office received only a six-page statement signed by the victim as well as Snapchat messages in which the men at the fraternity party advertised a free sexual encounter with Doe. State officials have also criticised Van Houten's decision not to bring charges or interview victims and witnesses himself. New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed the state's attorney general, Letitia James, to investigate the case. Kotlikoff said Cornell would be bringing in national sexual violence prevention experts to examine "the factors leading to campus sexual violence and strategies to promote responsible sexual citizenship". He said the steps were the first toward "systematic change" on campus.
